name: Omega-3 (EPA/DHA)
lead: Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated fats found in fish, fish oil, krill and algae, and the two long-chain forms, EPA and DHA, are among the most widely taken supplements in lifting, health and appearance circles [1][2][35]. People take them for skin that looks calmer and less dry, for lower soreness and better recovery between hard sessions, and as general anti-inflammatory support [4][5][39].

The mechanism offered is that EPA and DHA are built into cell membranes and converted to resolvins, protectins and related signalling molecules that help end inflammation, which proponents link to skin appearance and to training recovery [6][7]. The best-established regulatory use of purified EPA and DHA is lowering triglycerides in adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia, as stated on the US label for omega-3 acid ethyl esters [3].

Research on appearance outcomes is small: trials report reduced skin redness and blunted UV-induced prostaglandin E2 in healthy volunteers, a pilot trial in transplant recipients, and acne studies alongside isotretinoin [36][37][38][40]. Large cardiovascular analyses, including Cochrane reviews of 79 and 86 trials, found little or no effect on mortality or cardiovascular events [41].

paras: People take omega-3 fish oil, krill oil or algal oil for general skin health, and reviews and trials discuss it in relation to dry, red or inflamed skin [4][5][36]. Eating oily fish is the traditional route; capsules, liquids and algal products serve people who avoid fish [1][35].

The reasoning is a chain: EPA and DHA are built into cell membranes and feed the production of pro-resolving mediators that help switch inflammation off, which proponents link to calmer, less reactive skin and, for lifters, to less soreness and faster recovery [6][7][39].

A 2024 randomised trial tested fish-oil omega-3 combined with gamma-linolenic acid from blackcurrant seed oil in children with atopic dermatitis, and the paper notes earlier dermatitis studies gave mixed results [4]. Studies of fish oil alongside isotretinoin in acne have also been published, discussed below [40].

In lifting circles omega-3 is used as a recovery supplement, on the idea that less soreness lets people train more often and add muscle. Several trials have looked at muscle soreness after hard exercise, and a 2024 meta-analysis of four studies combined omega-3 with resistance training and found improved muscle strength but not muscle mass [12][39].

The US label for prescription omega-3 acid ethyl esters lists severe hypertriglyceridemia as its indication [3]. Wikipedia lists four fish-oil-derived prescription products approved by the FDA for high triglycerides, and notes one (Vascepa) received a 2019 approval to reduce cardiovascular risk alongside a statin [35].

Meta-analyses have examined omega-3 in ADHD in youths (small but significant symptom improvement), diabetes markers (reductions in fasting glucose and insulin resistance but not HbA1c) and resistance training for muscle strength [9][10][11][12]. Trials have combined a Mediterranean-style diet with fish oil in depression, and studied older adults' working memory, prostate cancer and endometriosis [13][14][15][16].

Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated fats with a double bond three carbons from the methyl end. The main types are alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), found in plants such as flax and chia, and the long-chain EPA and DHA from fish and algae [1]. Fish accumulate EPA and DHA by eating microalgae or prey fish, and oil content varies widely by species; salmon oil tends to be richer in DHA, while herring, mackerel, anchovy and sardine oils tend to be richer in EPA [35].

Supplements come as fish oil in capsules, softgels and gummies, krill oil, and less commonly algal oil. Krill oil carries omega-3s as phospholipids, and Wikipedia reports that krill oil has matched fish oil on blood lipids and inflammation markers at a lower EPA plus DHA content, while evidence on form and bioavailability is mixed [1][35]. Wikipedia describes humans converting ALA to EPA and DHA at under 5 percent, and notes that conversion is somewhat higher in women [1].

Wikipedia says supplement EPA and DHA content varies between products, based on ConsumerLab testing, and that oils oxidise easily, so freshness matters [1][35]. Cod liver oil is a separate product that also carries vitamins A and D [35].

Animals cannot make ALA and can convert it to EPA and then DHA only to a limited extent, which may decline with age [1]. EPA and DHA are incorporated into cell membranes and are precursors of resolvins, protectins and maresins, grouped as specialised pro-resolving mediators studied for roles in ending inflammation [6][7][17]. A 2010 paper identified GPR120 as an omega-3 receptor with anti-inflammatory and insulin-sensitising effects in cells [25].

The prescription label says the triglyceride-lowering mechanism is not completely understood and may involve reduced hepatic triglyceride synthesis [3]. Omega-6 and omega-3 fats compete for the same enzymes, which is why the omega-6 to omega-3 ratio of a diet is discussed; Wikipedia gives typical Western ratios of 10:1 to 30:1 and notes authors disagree on the ideal ratio [1][26].

A 2024 randomised trial in children with atopic dermatitis tested omega-3 with GLA [4]. Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials in healthy volunteers (55 people and 28 women) of a fish oil rich in cetoleic acid reported a higher omega-3 index and reduced skin erythema, which the authors described as an inflammation marker [36]. A 2004 double-blind trial in 28 people found 3 months of EPA abolished UV-B-induced skin prostaglandin E2, while the authors found no effect on the cytokines they measured and no evidence that EPA reduces sunburn through those cytokines [37].

A 12-month randomised pilot trial of omega-3 in 49 lung transplant recipients, who have a high skin cancer risk, found 6 skin cancers in the omega-3 group against 11 in placebo (odds ratio 0.34, confidence interval 0.09 to 1.32); the difference was not statistically significant and the authors called for a larger trial [38]. A registered immunonutrition trial also examined an omega-3 approach to skin cancer prevention [8].

In acne, a 2026 randomised, double-masked non-inferiority trial of 80 participants compared fish oil with placebo, each added to low-dose isotretinoin; acne counts were non-inferior between arms, and the fish oil group had smaller drops in skin hydration and smaller triglyceride rises [40]. A 2026 randomised trial of 46 patients with acne reported that omega-3 added to isotretinoin was associated with better clinical response and changes in lipid metabolism [40]. No large trial specifically testing EPA or DHA for wrinkles or skin texture was identified [17].

A 2020 meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials (145 supplement and 156 control participants) found significantly lower soreness after eccentric exercise with omega-3, but the effect was below the minimal clinically important difference and the authors rated the evidence low quality [39]. A 2021 systematic review of 15 studies found favourable effects on soreness and inflammatory markers but only one study meeting current quality recommendations [39]. Small trials since then, in 24 men and 15 female futsal players, reported lower soreness and faster strength recovery in supplemented groups [39]. A 2017 trial reported 33 to 42 percent smaller soreness effect sizes with fish oil that did not reach statistical significance [39]. The 2024 meta-analysis in resistance-trained people found strength gains but no change in muscle mass [12].

The evidence base is large. A 2002 American Heart Association statement reviewed fish consumption, fish oil and cardiovascular disease [18]. Cochrane reviews of 79 trials with 112,059 participants (2018) and 86 trials with 162,796 participants (2020) found little or no effect of long-chain omega-3 on all-cause mortality or cardiovascular events, a possible slight reduction in coronary heart disease events in the 2020 update, and about a 15 percent reduction in triglycerides [41].

Meta-analyses report a small effect on ADHD symptom scores in children (10 trials, 699 children in one analysis) and, in one 2022 review of 30 studies, reductions in fasting glucose and insulin resistance without a significant HbA1c effect [9][10][11]. A review of anti-inflammatory diets in rheumatoid arthritis rated its evidence very low [19]. Wikipedia describes a 2021 Cochrane depression review finding a small effect and no clinically meaningful benefit [1].
Registered trials include studies in type 2 diabetes, perioperative gastric cancer, muscle wasting and phospholipid versus conventional omega-3 formulations [20][21][22][23].

The US label for omega-3 acid ethyl esters lists belching, dyspepsia and altered taste as the most common reactions, and warns of possible LDL cholesterol increases, caution with fish or shellfish hypersensitivity, liver enzyme monitoring in hepatic impairment and a possible association with more frequent recurrence of symptomatic atrial fibrillation or flutter in people with prior atrial fibrillation [3]. Pregnancy data are described as insufficient to identify a drug-associated risk [3].

Wikipedia reports that the FDA advises limiting combined EPA and DHA to 3 grams a day from all sources and no more than 2 grams a day from supplements, that higher intakes may increase bleeding risk, that two 2021 reviews linked marine omega-3 above about 1 gram a day with atrial fibrillation, and that supplements can interact with blood-clotting drugs [1][35].

On contaminants, Wikipedia notes that mercury and lead tend to bind to fish protein rather than the oil, but PCBs, dioxins and similar compounds can be present, especially in less-refined oils, and that some brands exceeded PCB limits in 2006 [1][35]. Liver-based oils can carry high vitamin A [35]. A 2026 retrospective screening reported co-exposure to organohalogen contaminants through some fish oil supplements purchased in 2014 to 2017 [24]. Rancid oil may contain peroxides [35].

Fish oil was one of the earliest dietary supplements in the 1870s, and crude cod liver oil was used for rickets and other conditions in the late 1800s [35]. In 1929 George and Mildred Burr showed that fatty acids were essential nutrients and coined the term essential fatty acids [1]. Through the 1960s and 1970s, researchers described how omega-6 and omega-3 fats feed prostaglandin and related signalling molecules [1].

In 2004 the US FDA granted a qualified health claim that supportive but not conclusive research suggests EPA and DHA may reduce coronary heart disease risk; Canada permits a claim about DHA and brain, eye and nerve development in young children [1]. The American Heart Association position cited by Wikipedia is that 4 grams a day may lower triglycerides [1]. Prescription omega-3 products were approved for high triglycerides, and the omega-6 to omega-3 balance of Western diets has been discussed in the literature [3][26][35].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and lifting communities
paras: Omega-3 is a staple of general supplement stacks. On T Nation, omega-3 and fish oil appear in forum posts and staff articles as an anti-inflammatory foundation, with threads on DHA for men, mood, sleep and timing [27][28][29][30][31]. A July 2024 T Nation article by Chris Shugart presents DHA as reducing inflammation, soreness and appetite and as supporting lean mass; the article is published by a supplement company and promotes its own fish oil [30].

Supplements are regulated as foods in many countries, while prescription forms are drugs [3][35]. Wikipedia reports that by 2009 aquaculture used 81 percent of global fish oil supply, and that Antarctic krill catches are about 0.3 percent of unexploited biomass while krill are central to many marine food webs [1]. Algal oil is an alternative source of DHA [1].

lore.intro: On T Nation and in the wider lifting and appearance scene, omega-3 and fish oil are often presented as a foundational anti-inflammatory supplement, with threads on DHA for men, mood, sleep, skin and recovery [27][28][29][30][31].

claims.claim: Fish oil is a first-line anti-inflammatory supplement
claims.believers: T Nation articles state that inflammation underlies many unwanted conditions and that EPA and DHA from fish oil are the inflammation-fighting components, listing it among the first supplements to take [28][30].
claims.experts: Reviews describe pro-resolving mediators derived from EPA and DHA, but Wikipedia notes limited evidence for preventing most cardiovascular outcomes, cancer and all-cause mortality, and a review of anti-inflammatory diets in arthritis rated evidence very low [1][6][19].

claims.claim: Men need extra DHA because testosterone lowers DHA levels
claims.believers: A T Nation piece titled for "the manly omega-3" says testosterone lowers DHA levels and that most fish oils short-change men on DHA [32].
claims.experts: No trial identified tested a DHA-specific supplement for men on this premise.

claims.claim: High-dose DHA reduces sleep apnea events
claims.believers: A forum poster reports lowering apneas from 48 to 17 per hour using high doses of omega-3 DHA and links a PubMed paper on membrane DHA [33].
claims.experts: This is an individual report; no randomised trial confirms the result.

claims.believers: A T Nation article calls omega-3 a science-backed natural way to reduce anxiety, framing the issue as a basic deficiency [31].
claims.experts: Meta-analyses of other mental-health outcomes exist, for example modest ADHD symptom benefits in youths, while trials in depression pair fish oil with diet changes [9][13].

claims.claim: Omega-3 supports healthy telomeres and skin ageing
claims.believers: A T Nation article says inflammation is a main predator of telomeres and lists omega-3 among supplements to counter it [34].
claims.experts: Skin-specific trials are few; no study shows omega-3 supplementation slowing visible skin ageing.

claims.claim: Omega-3 reduces muscle soreness and speeds recovery
claims.believers: Supplement articles list DHA among nutrients that decrease muscle soreness and support lean mass gains [30].
claims.experts: A 2020 meta-analysis of 12 trials found a statistically significant reduction in soreness that was below the minimal clinically important difference, with low-quality evidence; a 2024 meta-analysis found strength but not muscle mass gains [12][39].

claims.claim: Most people are omega-3 deficient and need fish oil as a foundation
claims.believers: The July 2024 T Nation article says most Americans fall below optimal omega-3 levels and recommends DHA-rich fish oil as a base [30].
claims.experts: The Cochrane reviews found little or no effect of long-chain omega-3 on mortality or cardiovascular events, and Wikipedia notes limited benefit for most outcomes [1][41].

claims.claim: Omega-3 improves skin quality and calms skin inflammation
claims.believers: Supplement users say fish oil helps dry or reactive skin, citing its anti-inflammatory role [5][36].
claims.experts: Small trials report reduced erythema and blunted UV-induced prostaglandin E2, a pilot trial in transplant recipients was not statistically significant, and acne trials combined fish oil with isotretinoin [36][37][38][40].

claims.claim: A better omega-6 to omega-3 ratio is itself beneficial
claims.believers: Forum and article authors discuss cutting seed oils and raising fish intake to shift the ratio [26][28].
claims.experts: Reviews describe the ratio as influencing eicosanoid production, but Wikipedia reports authors disagree about the ideal ratio, from 1:1 to 4:1 [1][26].

angle.text: Fish oil, krill oil and algal oil are taken to support skin comfort and to reduce soreness so training can continue, with the reasoning running through inflammation. Small trials have measured reduced skin redness and soreness, and a meta-analysis found strength gains with resistance training [12][36][39].
